details:
**Lindisfarne raid (793)**
The Viking attack on the monastery of Lindisfarne, an island off the coast of Northumbria, traditionally marks the start of the Viking Age. It shocked Christian Europe, and the scholar Alcuin wrote letters mourning the attack, including one to Bishop Higbald of Lindisfarne. The monastery's famous Lindisfarne Gospels survived, though their jeweled cover was later lost, and the monks eventually fled with the relics of St. Cuthbert.

**Rollo and the Duchy of Normandy**
A Viking chieftain who, in the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte (911), received land around Rouen from the Frankish king Charles the Simple in exchange for defending it against other raiders and converting to Christianity. He was baptized as Robert and became the first ruler of Normandy. According to legend, when told to kiss the king's foot, Rollo's man lifted it to his mouth instead of bowing and tipped the king over. His descendants, the Normans, included William the Conqueror.

**Leif Erikson, Vinland, and L'Anse aux Meadows**
Around 1000 AD, Leif Erikson sailed west from Greenland and reached North America, naming one region Vinland ("wine land") for the grapes or berries found there. Excavations at L'Anse aux Meadows on the northern tip of Newfoundland revealed the only confirmed Norse site in the Americas. The Vinland sagas describe battles with Native peoples whom the Norse called Skraelings.

**Great Heathen Army and Alfred the Great**
A large Viking force, led by men such as Ivar the Boneless and traditionally called sons of Ragnar Lodbrok, invaded England in 865. They conquered most of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms and killed King Edmund of East Anglia, whose head they reportedly hid in a wood. Alfred the Great of Wessex resisted them at Ashdown, defeated Guthrum at Edington in 878, and built fortified towns called burhs.

**Danelaw**
The part of northern and eastern England under Viking control and Danish law, recognized in agreements between Alfred and Guthrum: the Treaty of Wedmore, under which Guthrum was baptized, and the later Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum. Scandinavian influence shows in local terms such as "wapentake" for a land division and "sokemen" for free landholders.

**Varangians and the Rus (Rurik)**
In Eastern Europe, Scandinavian traders and warriors, mostly from Sweden, were called Varangians or Rus and gave their name to Russia. Rurik is said to have taken control of Novgorod, and his kinsman Oleg took Kiev, founding Kievan Rus' and the Rurikid dynasty. The Arab traveler Ibn Fadlan described a Rus ship funeral on the Volga, and in 971 the Rus prince Sviatoslav was defeated by the Byzantines at Dorostolon.

**Varangian Guard**
The elite bodyguard of the Byzantine emperors, made up mostly of Scandinavians (and later many Anglo-Saxons), formed under Basil II in the late 900s. Varangians fought for the Byzantines in campaigns as far as Italy, including the Second Battle of Cannae in 1018.

**Danegeld, Maldon, and St. Brice's Day Massacre**
After Vikings defeated the English at the Battle of Maldon in 991, an event remembered in an Old English poem, King Æthelred the Unready paid huge tributes called Danegeld to buy them off. In 1002 he ordered the St. Brice's Day Massacre of Danes in England, which helped provoke further invasions by Sweyn Forkbeard. Archbishop Wulfstan's "Sermon of the Wolf to the English" treated these Viking attacks as God's punishment.

**Cnut (Canute) the Great**
The Danish king who conquered England in 1016 and also ruled Denmark and Norway, creating the "North Sea Empire." He married Emma of Normandy, Æthelred's widow, and went to Rome for the imperial coronation of Conrad II. His empire broke apart soon after his death in 1035.

**Battle of Clontarf (1014)**
A battle near Dublin in which the Irish High King Brian Boru, founder of the O'Brien dynasty, defeated the Norse of Dublin and their Leinster allies, though Brian himself was killed. In Ireland, Vikings had earlier set up fortified ship bases called longphorts, one of which grew into Dublin. They were also led by figures such as Turgesius, who, according to the annals, was captured and drowned by the Irish king Máel Sechnaill.

**Berserkers**
Norse warriors said to fight in a trance-like frenzy, sometimes without armor and wearing bear or wolf skins. The word may mean "bear-shirts." Questions also often note that Vikings did not actually wear horned helmets, a myth popularized in the 1800s.

**Longships and clinker building**
The Vikings' long, narrow, shallow-drafted ships, sometimes with dragon-headed prows. They could cross open seas and also sail up rivers for surprise raids inland. Their hulls were "clinker-built," made of overlapping planks fastened together. Important chiefs were sometimes buried in ships, as at Oseberg and Gokstad in Norway's Vestfold region.

**Erik the Red and Greenland**
Leif Erikson's father, who was banished from Iceland for killing and founded the Norse colonies in Greenland around 985. He gave the island an appealing name to attract settlers. His daughter Freydís Eiríksdóttir appears in the Vinland sagas, where she supposedly bared her breast and slapped it with a sword while pregnant to frighten off attacking Skraelings.

**Siege of Paris (845 and 885–886)**
Vikings sailed up the Seine and attacked Paris several times. In 845 Ragnar extracted a large ransom from Charles the Bald, an event recorded in sources such as the Annals of Xanten. The great siege of 885–886 was resisted by Count Odo and described in an eyewitness Latin poem by the monk Abbo Cernuus, and Emperor Charles the Fat finally bought the Vikings off.

**Viking women and shieldmaidens (Lagertha, Birka warrior)**
Saxo Grammaticus's Gesta Danorum describes the shieldmaiden Lagertha, who fought alongside Ragnar Lodbrok and became his wife. The "Birka female warrior" is a richly armed grave from the Swedish trading town of Birka, shown by DNA analysis to belong to a woman. It also contained a gaming board, which suggests she may have been a commander.
